title: Yasodhara's path
hookLine: the oldest rules call her only Rahula's mother; the commentaries remember her as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, foremost in great insight (AN 1)

cards: A name can disappear inside a relationship. In the Vinaya, when a small boy is sent to ask his father for his inheritance, the woman who sends him isn't called by her name. She's Rahulamata: Rahula's mother.

In year one we met her as Yasodhara, the wife the prince left sleeping, and we said her story doesn't end there. In those early pages she stands between two men: the husband who left, the son who followed him.
So what happens when the tradition tells her story as her own?

teach.b: First, what the old rules give her. In the Vinaya she appears without her name, as Rahula's mother, sending her son out to his father. It's a small part, and it leaves most of her life out.

The commentaries say that Yasodhara, too, went forth, after Mahapajapati opened the way, and that as a nun she was known as Bhadda Kaccana. The name Yasodhara belongs to the palace. Bhadda Kaccana belongs to the path.
Third, a title of her own.
In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of outstanding disciples, the Buddha names the nun Bhadda Kaccana foremost among those of great higher knowledge.

Read with the commentaries, that's Yasodhara, and the honor isn't for being a wife or a mother. It's for what she herself came to see, the same way Upali, Rahula and Mahapajapati were named: for her own quality.

teach.h: A FAREWELL IN HER OWN VOICE.
teach.b: Fourth, a farewell. A later collection of verses, the Apadana, gives her a voice at the end of her life. She goes to the Buddha to take her leave, and speaks of her long path in her own words, as one who has arrived.
It reads like a later text, full of wonders. But its point is plain. The woman once named only by her son is given her own last word.
Her awakening isn't a footnote to his.

how: In Theravada tradition Yasodhara is remembered through the commentaries and the Apadana as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, and some communities tell her story on its own terms, as a disciple who reached awakening.

o: her years of waiting alone in the palace
her own road as a nun, honored for her insight
the road she walked to bring Rahula home

p: her name as a nun, in the commentaries
gives her a farewell in her own voice

s: the oldest monastic rules tell Yasodhara's story in detail, by name
the Vinaya calls her only Rahula's mother; her fuller story comes from the commentaries and later texts.
the Anguttara names a nun, Bhadda Kaccana, foremost in great higher knowledge
and the commentaries identify Bhadda Kaccana with Yasodhara.
in the tradition, Yasodhara stays in the palace for the rest of her life
the commentaries say she went forth as a nun after the order of nuns began.

games.q: you're telling Yasodhara's story. the old rules name her only as Rahula's mother. where do you look for the rest of it?
o: nowhere: if the rules don't say it, it didn't happen.
the commentaries and the Apadana, read as later texts.
games.why: the commentaries name her as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, and the later Apadana gives her a farewell in her own voice. later, and full of wonders, but hers.

practice: Bring to mind someone usually introduced through someone else: somebody's wife, somebody's mother, somebody's assistant, somebody's younger brother.

Set the relationship aside and see them on their own: what have they come to know that's theirs, what road did they walk without anyone watching? Say their own name silently a few times, and breathe with them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Yasodhara's path. Called Rahula's mother in the old rules, remembered by the commentaries as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, foremost in great knowledge. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Yasodhara: her name in the palace. As a nun, the commentaries call her Bhadda Kaccana.

carryVoice: Your line: her own awakening. Her name, her path, her own last word. Day seven hundred fifty-four, done.
